subject: unilateral-mistake
note:
TEN FORKS, NONE MATERIALISED AS AN INTERPRETATION FIELD, and one materialised as a REFUSE. R4's Interpretation-record machinery was not used: this corpus's live ambiguities are not places where one module should compute two answers, they are places where a JURISDICTION has not decided -- and the honest encoding of that is a refusal (F-EW1), not a parameter. The five `delegated-to-fact` entries are the other pattern: a contestable CHARACTERISATION of a decided case's facts, delegated to the fixture, where two of them (F-US2, F-C3) are exercised explicitly by a labelled counterfactual fixture that moves that one field and asserts the result.

THIS REGISTER IS NOT CLAIMED TO BE COMPLETE. Fork completeness is unfalsifiable in principle, and it is weaker here than in a statute corpus for a specific reason: three of the four jurisdictions were read through a single Singapore judgment's account of them, so an ambiguity visible only in the English, Australian or American reports could not have been seen from here at all. See NOTES.md section 3.

site.anchor: the gap Great Peace Shipping left
provisions: Great Peace Shipping Ltd v Tsavliris Salvage (International) Ltd [2003] QB 679
Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [74]

source.quote: had accepted that the equitable remedy of rescission for unilateral mistake still survived Great Peace Shipping

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [74], citing Huyton SA v Distribuidora Internacional de Productos Agricolas SA de CV [2003] 2 Lloyd's Rep 780 and Harrison v Halliwell Landau [2004] EWHC 1316

readings.description: The equitable jurisdiction to rescind for unilateral mistake survived Great Peace Shipping, which concerned common mistake only. Two English High Court decisions have so held.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [74]

readings.description: Great Peace Shipping swept away the equitable jurisdiction in mistake generally, unilateral included -- the reading the Singapore High Court adopted below.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2004] SGHC 71, as characterised in the Court of Appeal at [62] and [80]

taken.rationale: NEITHER reading is taken, and that is the point. Both are live and no English appellate court has chosen between them, so the module REFUSES on the class of facts where the choice matters rather than picking one. `taken.reading` names `survives` only because the schema requires a value; read `mechanism: refused` as the operative field. This is the corpus's only materialised fork and its only REFUSE.

notes: WHAT CHANGES IF THE OTHER READING IS TAKEN: On the two fixtures that fall in this class -- Digilandmall's second appellant and Taylor v Johnson -- the England column reads a refusal where Singapore reads `voidable`. On the `abolished` reading it would read `stands`; on the `survives` reading it would probably read `voidable`, though on what conditions is itself unsettled.

SCHEMA GAP, RECORDED RATHER THAN WORKED AROUND SILENTLY. `taken.mechanism` admits only TYPICALLY, encoded and fact-supplied, so there is no value meaning 'neither reading was taken; the encoding REFUSES'. `encoded` is used because the refusal genuinely is encoded -- ew-unilateral-mistake.l4 carries a REFUSE whose name is its message -- but a reader should not take `taken.reading: survives` at face value: NO reading was adopted. The schema predates the REFUSE construct and a `refused` mechanism would let this be said directly. This is a candidate upstream issue against specs/todo/single-instruction-demo/schemas/fork-register.schema.json.
witnesses: `what English law does` `Digilandmall -- the second appellant` -- refuses; Singapore reads voidable
`what English law does` `Taylor v Johnson` -- refuses; Singapore and Australia both read voidable

site.anchor: the verdict -- voidable, and never void
provisions: Taylor v Johnson (1983) 151 CLR 422
Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [73]

source.quote: To the extent that the majority judgment seems to suggest that the contract would not be void even where the non-mistaken party knew of a fundamental mistake, we would hesitate to adopt a similar position.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [73]

readings.description: Taylor v Johnson routes every unilateral mistake to equity, so Australian law has no common law `void` outcome for it. The contract is voidable or nothing.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [73]

readings.description: A common law doctrine voiding a contract for an actually-known fundamental mistake survives in Australia alongside Taylor v Johnson, which decided only what equity does.

citations.cite: Not established from any retrieved source. The Commonwealth Law Reports were not consulted; this reading is recorded because the Singapore court's own hedge -- 'seems to suggest' -- leaves it open.

taken.rationale: Taken because it is what the retrieved source states, and rejected-in-passing by that same source. THIS IS THE HIGHEST-CONSEQUENCE CHARACTERISATION IN THE CORPUS: it produces three `stands` cells where Singapore and England both void, and it rests on one hedged sentence of a Singapore judgment about an Australian one. NOTES.md section 6 lists it as the first thing a reviewer should attack.

notes: WHAT CHANGES IF THE OTHER READING IS TAKEN: Under `voidLimbSurvives`, Australia would read `void` on Digilandmall's third appellant and on Hartog, agreeing with Singapore and England instead of diverging, and half of Delta 2 would disappear.
RELATED FORKS (recorded here because `cross_refs` addresses the external-modifications register, not this one): F-AU2.
witnesses: `what Taylor v Johnson does` `Digilandmall -- the third appellant` -- stands, against void in Singapore and England
`what Taylor v Johnson does` `Hartog v Colin and Shields` -- stands, against void in Singapore and England

provisions: Taylor v Johnson (1983) 151 CLR 422 at 432
Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [73]

source.quote: What is less clear is whether it was an essential element for equity to intervene that the non-mistaken party must

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [73]

readings.description: Deliberately setting out to prevent the mistaken party discovering the mistake is an ESSENTIAL element of the Taylor v Johnson test; mere silence does not engage it.

citations.cite: Taylor v Johnson (1983) 151 CLR 422 at 432, as quoted in Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [73]

readings.description: The deliberate conduct in Taylor v Johnson was how equity was engaged on those facts, not a necessary condition -- so a conscious omission would engage it too, and Australia would not differ from Singapore here at all.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [73], which raises exactly this doubt and does not resolve it for Australian law

readings.foreclosure: Foreclosed by the words of the test as the High Court stated them and as Chwee Kin Keong at [73] quotes them: the element is expressed as something the non-mistaken party must have done, not as one illustration among others. The Singapore court's doubt is doubt about whether that SHOULD be the test, not a finding that it is not.

taken.rationale: Taken because it is the test as the High Court stated it, and because taking the other reading would make the Australian module a copy of the Singapore one and the comparison vacuous. The Singapore court's doubt about it is quoted in full at the site.

notes: WHAT CHANGES IF THE OTHER READING IS TAKEN: Under `deliberateStepsIllustrative`, Australia relieves on Digilandmall's second appellant and Delta 1 -- the corpus's headline finding -- disappears entirely.
RELATED FORKS (recorded here because `cross_refs` addresses the external-modifications register, not this one): F-AU1.
witnesses: `what Taylor v Johnson does` `Digilandmall -- the second appellant` -- stands, against voidable in Singapore; this is Delta 1

site.anchor: the mistake is of a kind the doctrine reaches
provisions: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [34]
Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd [2020] SGCA(I) 02 at [13(a)], [80] and [92]

source.quote: It was not necessary in this case for the CA to determine whether unilateral mistake in equity could extend beyond a mistake as to a term of the contract

citations.cite: Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd [2020] SGCA(I) 02 at [13(a)], reporting that court at [80] and [92]

readings.description: Both limbs are confined to a mistake as to a term of the contract.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [34]; Quoine at [13(a)]

readings.description: Equity, being the more elastic jurisdiction, may reach a fundamental mistake that is not as to a term -- expressly left open.

citations.cite: Quoine at [80] and [92], reserving the point; Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [75], canvassing a 'wider and perhaps open-ended category of fundamental mistake'

taken.rationale: Taken because it is what both cases decided on, and because the alternative has never been applied. If it were taken, Singapore would reach the Quoine facts and the sharpest US/SG divergence would narrow.

notes: WHAT CHANGES IF THE OTHER READING IS TAKEN: Under `equityReachesFurther`, the Quoine counterfactual fixture and possibly Smith v Hughes would move in the Singapore column, and the modelling choice recorded as F-C4 becomes load-bearing.
RELATED FORKS (recorded here because `cross_refs` addresses the external-modifications register, not this one): F-C4.
witnesses: `what Singapore law does` `Quoine -- counterfactual, enforcement unconscionable` -- stands, against voidable under the Restatement
`what Singapore law does` `Smith v Hughes` -- stands, on the term/assumption line alone

site.anchor: what is encoded, and from where
provisions: Restatement (Second) of Contracts ss 153 and 154
Donovan v RRL Corp (2001) 26 Cal 4th 261

source.quote: Because the rule in section 153, subdivision (a), of the Restatement Second of Contracts, authorizing rescission for unilateral mistake of fact where enforcement would be unconscionable, is consistent with our previous decisions, we adopt the rule as California law.

citations.cite: Donovan v RRL Corp (2001) 26 Cal 4th 261

readings.description: Encode the Restatement rule itself, and label the column as the Restatement rather than as 'the United States'.

citations.cite: Restatement (Second) of Contracts s 153, as quoted in Donovan v RRL Corp

readings.description: Encode California law, which adopted s 153(a) but reaches s 153(b) through its own line of authority.
readings.rejection_rationale: Only one Californian case was retrieved, which is not enough to state a State's law, and doing so would claim a survey that was never performed.

taken.rationale: The Restatement binds nobody until a State adopts it, and adoption is uneven. Every row of the comparison table that turns on the American column should be read as 'the Restatement rule', which is what the module's @export description says.

entries.delegated_field: the mistaken party bears the risk of the mistake

provisions: Restatement (Second) of Contracts s 154(b)
Smith v Hughes (1871) LR 6 QB 597

source.quote: he is aware, at the time the contract is made, that he has only limited knowledge with respect to the facts to which the mistake relates but treats his limited knowledge as sufficient

citations.cite: Restatement (Second) of Contracts s 154(b), as quoted in Donovan v RRL Corp

readings.description: A buyer who inspects a sample of the oats and forms his own view of their age treats limited knowledge as sufficient, and bears the risk under s 154(b).

citations.cite: Restatement (Second) of Contracts s 154(b), as quoted in Donovan v RRL Corp: a party bears the risk where 'he is aware, at the time the contract is made, that he has only limited knowledge with respect to the facts to which the mistake relates but treats his limited knowledge as sufficient'

readings.description: The buyer's mistake was induced by the transaction's circumstances rather than by his own decision to rely on a sample, so s 154 does not allocate the risk to him.

citations.cite: Restatement (Second) of Contracts s 154, whose three limbs are exhaustive: on this reading none of (a), (b) or (c) is engaged, and the section allocates risk only where one of them is

readings.foreclosure: Foreclosed on these facts by the buyer's own inspection of a sample, which is the paradigm of treating limited knowledge as sufficient under s 154(b). It stays arguable because no American court has decided Smith v Hughes and the characterisation is this model's.

taken.rationale: This model's reading, not a holding: no American court has decided Smith v Hughes. It is the only thing keeping the American column from diverging on that fixture, so fixture 6a moves this one field and nothing else, and asserts the result.

notes: WHAT CHANGES IF THE OTHER READING IS TAKEN: Under `buyerDoesNotBearRisk`, the United States relieves on Smith v Hughes and the four-way agreement on that row breaks -- which is exactly what fixture 6a demonstrates.
witnesses: `what the Restatement does` `Smith v Hughes` -- stands, against `Smith v Hughes -- counterfactual, risk not borne`, which is voidable on this one field

provisions: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [93] and [98]

source.quote: Clearly suspecting a mistake, he pounced on the opportunity to make more money before the mistake was discovered.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [93]

readings.description: He said nothing and moved fast. Haste is not concealment, and the court warned that 'haste per se in concluding a transaction will not ipso facto suggest actual or constructive knowledge'.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [98]

readings.description: Ordering 760 printers at speed specifically to complete before the seller noticed IS a course of conduct designed to inhibit discovery.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [93], 'before the mistake was discovered'

readings.foreclosure: Foreclosed by Chwee Kin Keong at [98], where the court warned that haste in concluding a transaction does not by itself establish knowledge or design. Speed to complete is not the same as a course of conduct aimed at preventing discovery.

taken.rationale: Taken on the court's own warning at [98] that haste is not itself knowledge or design. The stronger reading would make Australia relieve and erase the divergence this fixture exists to show, which is a reason to record it prominently rather than a reason to prefer it.

notes: WHAT CHANGES IF THE OTHER READING IS TAKEN: Under `deliberateSteps`, Australia reads `voidable` instead of `stands` on this fixture.
RELATED FORKS (recorded here because `cross_refs` addresses the external-modifications register, not this one): F-AU2.
witnesses: `what Taylor v Johnson does` `Digilandmall -- the third appellant` -- stands under `consciousOmission`, voidable under `deliberateSteps`

entries.delegated_field: the mistaken party bears the risk of the mistake

provisions: Riverlate Properties Ltd v Paul [1975] Ch 133
Restatement (Second) of Contracts s 154(c)

source.quote: the error was purely that of the lessor and/or its solicitors

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [70], summarising Riverlate

readings.description: A court would reasonably allocate to the lessor the risk of its own solicitors' drafting omission, under s 154(c).

citations.cite: Russell LJ at 141, quoted at [70]: equity should not disrupt a transaction where the other party's conscience was clear

readings.description: Nothing allocated the risk, and the omission was a clerical slip rather than an accepted uncertainty.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [70], recording that the lessor 'had mistakenly omitted to insert a clause' -- an omission, not an accepted uncertainty, and so outside Restatement s 154(b)

readings.foreclosure: Foreclosed by Russell LJ at 141, quoted at [70]: where the other party's conscience was clear, equity should not disrupt the transaction. A court asked to allocate the risk under s 154(c) would be answering that same question.

taken.rationale: Taken because Russell LJ's reasoning is squarely that the bargain should stand, which is the same judgement s 154(c) asks a court to make. It is what keeps the American column from diverging on the corpus's control case, so the control case is only as strong as this reading.

notes: WHAT CHANGES IF THE OTHER READING IS TAKEN: Under `lessorDoesNotBearRisk`, the United States would ask whether enforcement was unconscionable; on this record it was not, so the row would probably not move -- but it would then turn on a second contested characterisation instead of one.
witnesses: `what the Restatement does` `Riverlate Properties v Paul` -- stands; the only fixture on which all four agree, and it agrees because of this reading

site.anchor: 8 -- Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd
provisions: Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd [2020] SGCA(I) 02

source.quote: a mistaken assumption that the Platform would not fail

citations.cite: Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd [2020] SGCA(I) 02 at [16]

readings.description: Enforcing trades between two sophisticated market-makers on an exchange whose own rules governed aberrant values is not unconscionable, and no court has said it is.

citations.cite: Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd [2020] SGCA(I) 02 at [16], which characterises the counterparties' error as 'a mistaken assumption that the Platform would not fail' and records no finding of unconscionability anywhere in the case

readings.description: Enforcing a trade struck at roughly 250 times the market rate, produced by the platform's own failure, would be unconscionable.

citations.cite: Restatement (Second) of Contracts s 153(a), which asks only whether 'the effect of the mistake is such that enforcement of the contract would be unconscionable' -- a question about the bargain, which a trade at roughly 250 times the market rate squarely raises

readings.foreclosure: Foreclosed by the absence of any judicial characterisation: no court has called these trades unconscionable, and both parties were sophisticated market-makers on an exchange whose own rules addressed aberrant values.

taken.rationale: Taken because no court has characterised these trades as unconscionable and this model will not be the first. Fixture 8a moves the field explicitly, is labelled COUNTERFACTUAL, and exists so the reading can be seen rather than assumed.

notes: WHAT CHANGES IF THE OTHER READING IS TAKEN: Under `unconscionable`, the Restatement relieves on facts Singapore's doctrine cannot reach at all, because the mistake was not as to a term -- which is fixture 8a and the cleanest statement of what the term/assumption line costs.
RELATED FORKS (recorded here because `cross_refs` addresses the external-modifications register, not this one): F-SG1.
witnesses: `what the Restatement does` `Quoine v B2C2` -- stands, against `Quoine -- counterfactual, enforcement unconscionable`, which is voidable on this one field

site.anchor: the mistake was fundamental, on non-term fixtures
provisions: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [34]

source.quote: It has to be a sufficiently important or fundamental mistake as to a term for that to happen.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [34]

readings.description: On a mistake that is not as to a term, `the mistake was fundamental` is set FALSE, encoding 'the predicate is not engaged'.

citations.cite: Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com Pte Ltd [2005] SGCA 2 at [34]: 'It has to be a sufficiently important or fundamental mistake as to a term for that to happen' -- fundamentality is defined by reference to a term, so on a non-term mistake there is nothing for it to qualify

readings.description: Model fundamentality as an optional value so that 'not engaged' and 'engaged and false' are distinguishable.

citations.cite: No legal source: this reading is about the ENCODING, not about the law. It is arguable on ordinary modelling grounds -- MAYBE BOOLEAN would distinguish 'not engaged' from 'engaged and false' -- and is recorded so the collapse is visible.

readings.foreclosure: Foreclosed for now by the term test failing ahead of it in every rule that reads both fields, so the distinction is unobservable. It stops being foreclosed the day F-SG1 resolves in favour of `equityReachesFurther`.

taken.rationale: Fundamentality in the Singapore sense is defined BY REFERENCE TO a term, so on a non-term mistake there is nothing for it to be true or false about. FALSE is safe only because the term test fails ahead of it in every rule that reads both. If F-SG1 is ever resolved the other way, this choice becomes load-bearing and must be revisited.

notes: None today; the field is unreachable on the fixtures where it is set this way.
RELATED FORKS (recorded here because `cross_refs` addresses the external-modifications register, not this one): F-SG1.

Broadley Construction Pte Ltd v Alacran Design Pte Ltd [2018] SGCA 25
Axis Megalink Sdn Bhd v Far East Mining Pte Ltd [2024] SGHC(A) 15

source.quote: were satisfied, namely that for a unilateral mistake

citations.cite: Broadley Construction Pte Ltd v Alacran Design Pte Ltd [2018] SGCA 25, found by the sweep and not read
Axis Megalink Sdn Bhd v Far East Mining Pte Ltd [2024] SGHC(A) 15 at [77], found by the sweep and not read

readings.description: Chwee Kin Keong as restated in Quoine (2020) is the whole of the Singapore test, and the later decisions apply it without refining it.

citations.cite: Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd [2020] SGCA(I) 02 at [13], which restates the test in the same terms fifteen years on

readings.description: One or more of the three Singapore decisions found but not read has refined the test -- most plausibly Broadley, a Court of Appeal decision, or Axis Megalink, the most recent.
readings.foreclosure: Foreclosed only by the fact that Quoine, the most authoritative later decision and the one that WAS read, restates the test unchanged. That is real but partial evidence: it says nothing about the two decisions handed down after it.

citations.cite: Broadley Construction Pte Ltd v Alacran Design Pte Ltd [2018] SGCA 25 -- a Court of Appeal decision applying the requirements, whose treatment of them was not read
Axis Megalink Sdn Bhd v Far East Mining Pte Ltd [2024] SGHC(A) 15 at [77] -- the most recent authority found, discussing the doctrine's rationale, not read

taken.rationale: Taken because Quoine was read in full and restates the test unchanged. THIS FORK EXISTS BECAUSE THE SWEEP WAS INCOMPLETE, not because the law is doubtful: three later Singapore decisions were found and not read. It is the register's honest record of an unmet obligation, and it is the reason the three `deferred` entries in external-modifications.json are deferred rather than dispositioned `no-effect`.

notes: Closing this fork is cheap and mechanical: read three judgments. It is listed in NOTES.md section 6 as work a reviewer can discharge without any special access.
